=== Tract Post-Workshop Comments on Staff's Second Discussion Draft - 58481.pdf ===
                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §                  BEFORE THE
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                     §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                  §
                                                §                    OF TEXAS


  TRACT HOLDING COMPANY I, LLC’S POST-WORKSHOP COMMENTS ON STAFF’S
       SECOND DISCUSSION DRAFT RULE TO IMPLEMENT LARGE LOAD
                    INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
Introduction

Tract Holding Company I, LLC, on behalf of its affiliates, (“Tract”) appreciates the invitation to
submit post-workshop comments on key issues being addressed in this rulemaking. Tract,
through its affiliates, acquires land and develops shovel-ready development sites for data
centers—pre-positioning power, fiber, zoning, and entitlements—to expedite speed to power and
provide data center operators with faster build cycles at lower risk. Tract is actively developing
several such projects in Texas and currently has 2.8 gigawatts of proposed projects in advanced
stages of development in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (“ERCOT”) Large Load
Interconnection Study (“LLIS”) process (composed of four projects across three Transmission
Service Providers (“TSPs”)), with more in development. In response to requests from Public
Utility Commission of Texas (“PUCT” or “Commission”) staff at the workshop held January 9th,
2026, Tract provides these comments to recommend five important modifications to the second
discussion draft.
   1. The final rule in Project 58481 should only apply to projects requesting
      interconnection after the adoption of the new standards. In no event should the rule
      apply to projects that have already been engaged in the planning process and have
      LLIS numbers assigned before the date of adoption of the final rule.

Tract’s priority concern is that projects in development prior to the rule becoming effective
should not be negatively impacted by the retroactive application of this rule. Through Senate
Bill 6 (“SB 6”) from 2025, the Texas Legislature and Governor evinced their intent by explicitly
stating that “the standards must apply only to customers requesting a new or expanded
interconnection.” Texas Utilities Code Section 37.0561(c) (emphasis added). This plain language
would require the new standards being developed here to be applied only to projects requesting
“new or expanded” interconnection after the date of adoption of the new rule. The plain language
of SB 6 also states that these are standards the PUCT must implement by rule; they are not
requirements applicable as of the effective date of the underlying bill (i.e. June 20, 2025) or
some other date (e.g. September 1, 2025 is a date applicable to the net metering review
requirements in SB 6). See Texas Utilities Code 37.0561(b).

                                                1
 When serious projects begin the process of entering the ERCOT market, significant decisions,
including financial resource commitments, are made based on the rules in place at the time. To
change these rules for projects already in advanced stages of development will have a negative
impact on businesses and send a negative market signal that will deter future business
development, counter to the intent of SB 6. See Texas Utilities Code Section 37.0561(b). If the
Commission believes it must apply these standards to existing load interconnection requests,
contrary to the plain language of SB 6, the new standards adopted by this rule should not apply
to projects that are so far along the existing process that they have already been assigned an LLIS
number by ERCOT.

Moreover, applying these standards only to newly submitted requests after the adoption date has
the added benefit of avoiding confusion with the ongoing Batch Study Process ERCOT is
developing. The Batch 0 criteria and batching process can be applied to existing requests and
new requests going forward, while these standards would apply only to new requests submitted
after the standards are adopted. Doing so avoids confusion and reduces the burden and
complexity faced by developers, utilities, PUCT, and ERCOT that would result if existing
requests are required to meet the Batch requirements this Spring in addition to these standards
just a few months later in June.

In contrast, introducing new burdens on late-stage projects imposes additional costs, can create
delays, and will potentially harm businesses, strand investment, and discourage future
investment, contrary to the goals of SB 6. This rulemaking process itself should not become a
cause of delay in projects moving forward under the existing system. Tract is especially
concerned about the new rule causing restudy of projects previously studied or in the process of
being studied. Causing restudies would not reduce the queue, but rather increase the backlog of
the queue and related delays.

Suggested Language:

Addition of new "Applicability" subsection in 25.194(b), which changes all subsequent
subsection lettering to one letter later in the alphabet:

Option 1:
(b) Applicability
The standards and criteria for an electric utility, a municipally owned utility and electric
cooperative, to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network
established under this Section shall apply only to new or expanded requests submitted to the
Interconnecting Utility after the standards and criteria are adopted by the Commission.



                                                2
 Option 2:
(b) Applicability
The standards and criteria for an electric utility, a municipally owned utility and electric
cooperative, to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network
established under this Section shall apply only to new or expanded requests that have not
received a Large Load Interconnection Study number from ERCOT as of the date when the
standards and criteria are adopted by the Commission.


   2. The rule should allow surety bonds as an acceptable form of payment for financial
      security.
In the second staff discussion draft, PUC Subst. R. 25.194(f)(8)(C) lists the acceptable forms for
the required financial security. Tract recommends that surety bonds be added to this list. Surety
bonds are a proven method of providing financial security and are accepted by ERCOT and other
utilities and market operators across the country. This addition will meet the dual objectives of
supporting business development and lowering infrastructure costs.
Suggested Language:
Addition of surety bond in 25.194(f)(8)(C) and 25.194(i)(8)(B):
(iv) a surety bond issued by a major institution with a credit rating of at least "A-" by Standard &
Poor's or "A3" by Moody's Investor Service or an equivalent rating.
   3. The rule should not distinguish between project developer and end-use customer.
The second discussion draft requires a large load applicant for interconnection to disclose to the
Interconnecting Utility whether the customer is a project developer or an end-use customer.
There is no statutory basis for collection of this information, and the simple separation of the two
general categories of interconnection applicant is not meaningful. There is a spectrum of
potential business structures that may apply as the market spurs innovation by parties striving to
find efficiencies or competitive advantages in the development process. The variety of potential
arrangements is significant and changing, and it is not confined to the two options identified by
the discussion draft.
Based on the discussion at the workshop, there is no purpose to this reporting requirement other
than “information gathering,” for parties that would project their own imaginings on these
categories, and Tract shares the concern of several other commenters at the workshop that the
very collection of such information provides the potential for it to be misused. Tract contends
that distinguishing a project developer from an end-use customer without purpose simply opens
the door to potential discrimination for project advancement. Tract suggests that the definitions
and disclosure requirements be removed from the rule in sections (b)(4), (b)(12), (c)(1), (f)(1),
and (i)(1) as proposed. Because the information required for in the discussion draft is not

                                                 3
 required by SB 6, serves no discernible purpose, and invites potential discriminatory treatment, it
should be stricken from the draft rule.
Suggested Language:
   Delete 25.194(b)(4) and (12); 25.194(c)(1); 25.194(f)(1); 25.194(i)(1)
   4. The timeline for the return of posted financial security should follow actual costs
      recovered from the projects.
The discussion draft proposal requires the Interconnecting Utility to return 20% of the remaining
balance of posted financial security when the large load customer energizes and ratably as the
large load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer' s schedule for phased
energization of its contracted peak demand. The Interconnecting Utility must then return any
remaining balance when the large load customer sustains operations for five years at the
customer' s contracted peak. The return of posted financial security five years after 100%
energization is an unnecessarily long time. There are two issues of concern with this approach.
First, several parties noted in their comments that large load facilities are designed with a
capacity that they expect to achieve very rarely in the sense that, for example, they may only
achieve on an exceptionally hot day in an unusual year. That is the nature of design; projects are
developed to handle extreme cases, and it may be years before the facility reaches its 100% peak
demand. Financial security should be returned to the customer as the costs that the financial
security was protecting against no longer pose a risk (e.g., stranded costs or shifting of costs).
After the initial 20% is returned to the customer, the remaining financial security should be
returned based on the transmission charges paid by the interconnecting large load, or within five
years, whichever happens first.
There is no reason to delay return of financial security for five years past when transmission
charges paid by the large load customer to the Interconnecting Utility equal or exceed the
financial security provided. It should also be noted that there was considerable discussion about
the intent of the rule with respect to its impact on the traditional “postage stamp rate,” where
customers pay for the cost of their transmission services through their tariffed rates with the
Interconnecting Utility. The discussion draft proposal implies a significant change from the
current approach which, together with the competitive electric market, has sustained the
economic growth of the state in recent decades. Tract supports other parties that emphasize the
preference for maintaining this status quo. To the extent that additional costs are foisted upon
large loads, beyond those historically considered the “direct cost” of interconnection, and beyond
those that non large load customers bear, the extended time requirements to return financial
security are even more unnecessary. Financial security returned for a project which has
completed its full facility build out and paid for its cost of interconnection through transmission
charges, is financial security that can be used to develop additional projects. If the commission
adopts language to support the current cost allocation for transmission in the tariff rates, then at
the very least Tract agrees with the Data Center Coalition that a project should receive return of

                                                 4
 its posted financial security at the end of the proposed five years or when it has paid the cost
associated with its interconnection through those rates, whichever comes first.
Suggested Language:
Edit 25.194(l)(1):
   After applying the financial security to any amounts owed, the Interconnecting Utility must
   return 20% of the remaining balance when the large load customer energizes and ratably as
   the large load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer's schedule for phased
   energization of its contracted peak large load customer pays transmission charges to the
   Interconnecting Utility.
   5. Transparency.
Anything that can be done to provide visibility into the study process is helpful. Today, the
opaque nature of the application evaluation process is a primary barrier to project commitment
by developers. The proposed discussion draft largely focuses on the requirements for large
loads, but not their rights or access to information on the modeling used in the process. For
example, requiring not only that the Interconnecting Utility alert the load applicant when its
study is complete (section (e)(4)), but also sharing the study and underlying evaluation files
themselves within a reasonable time would be helpful so the developer can understand what, if
anything, can be done to reduce delay or cost. Doing so supports the dual objectives of SB 6 to
support business development and reduce infrastructure costs.
   6. Load Flexibility and Evaluation of Available Capacity: Customer Rights.
Although there is language in the discussion draft to require disclosure of the nature and
responsiveness of on-site backup generating facilities (as defined in the draft), there is no
mention of what such responsiveness might enable in the load interconnection process. While
this issue might be resolved in the ERCOT stakeholder process, the Commission can provide
leadership by providing direction that the interconnecting large load applicant has the right to be
evaluated as a flexible load. That is, a large load with the technical capacity to reliably reduce its
load, or curtail demand entirely, in response to a market signal should be evaluated in line with
its actual impact on the market or the grid. A load that can respond to energy availability when
resource shortages occur, as signaled by Security Constrained Economic Dispatch (“SCED”),
should be able to request (voluntarily) to be evaluated as a non-firm load for determination of the
available capacity. Similarly, a large load that can provide the capacity to reduce or curtail
demand pre- or even post-contingency, sufficiently quickly so as not to be a factor after failure of
a transmission system element, will have no impact on the N-1 or N-1-1 reliability calculation.
The evaluation of capacity available for interconnection of such a fast-responding load resource
should reflect this capacity, and the development of the ERCOT interconnection process should
evolve to make this possible. Neither of these options need to be considered as permanent
solutions. Both of these options can allow much faster integration of additional loads as the

                                                  5
 transmission network is being built out. This supports the objectives of SB 6 to support business
development, reduce infrastructure costs, and maintain system reliability.
Conclusion
Tract appreciates consideration of these important comments as the Proposal for Publication is
being developed.
                                                            Respectfully Submitted,



                                                            Orijit Ghoshal
                                                            Vice President, Government and
                                                            Regulatory Affairs
                                                            3200 Cherry Creek S Drive
                                                            Denver, CO 80209
